challenges.name: secrets-oidc-quiz
challenges.title: Read the security review findings
challenges.description: Three statements about workflows the security review flagged in Rice Rocket's repository. Decide whether each one is true.
hints: With `pull_request_target`, separate two things: where the workflow file comes from, and whose code the steps actually execute after the checkout.
The `sub` claim of GitHub's OIDC token names the repository plus the environment, the ref, or `pull_request`. Which of those forms does the pattern `repo:rice-rocket/app:*` match?
When `permissions:` is a map, what happens to every scope the map does not name? Then look at what `actions/checkout` needs to read a private repository.

questions.question:
A workflow posts test coverage to a service on every pull request, forks included:

```yaml
on: pull_request_target
jobs:
  coverage:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
      - run: npm ci && npm test -- --coverage
        working-directory: api
        env:
          COVERAGE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.COVERAGE_TOKEN }}
```

Statement: "This is safe: with `pull_request_target` the workflow file always comes from the base branch, so a fork cannot change what runs."
questions.explanation: False. The workflow file is the base branch's, but its second step runs the fork's code: `npm ci` runs the install scripts of the fork's `package.json`, and `npm test` runs the fork's test files, all with `COVERAGE_TOKEN` in the environment and a token that can write to the base repository. This is the "pwn request" pattern. Run untrusted code under `pull_request` (no secrets for forks), and if a privileged step must follow, run it in a separate `workflow_run` workflow that never executes the pull request's code. The misconception is that controlling the YAML means controlling everything it executes.

questions.question:
The IAM role that deploys the web site trusts GitHub's OIDC provider with these conditions:

```json
"Condition": {
  "StringEquals": { "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com" },
  "StringLike": { "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:rice-rocket/app:*" }
}
```

```text
sub claims seen in CloudTrail last week
repo:rice-rocket/app:environment:production
repo:rice-rocket/app:ref:refs/heads/feature/momo-pay
repo:rice-rocket/app:pull_request
```

Statement: "Any workflow run in `rice-rocket/app` that asks for `id-token: write` can assume this role, including one on a feature branch or a `pull_request` run from a branch of the same repository; `repo:rice-rocket/app:environment:production` would limit it to jobs that use the production environment."
questions.explanation: True. `*` matches every subject the repository can produce: environment, branch or tag ref, and `pull_request`. Anyone who can push a branch can write a workflow that requests an ID token and assumes the production role. When a job references an environment, the `sub` becomes `repo:<owner>/<repo>:environment:<name>`, so matching that exact value ties the role to the environment, whose protection rules (required reviewers, deployment branches) then guard the credentials. The misconception is that the repository name alone is a strong enough boundary.

questions.question:
A new deploy workflow sets only the OIDC permission at the top. The repository is private:

```yaml
permissions:
  id-token: write
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
```

```text
Run actions/checkout@v5
  remote: Repository not found.
  Error: fatal: repository 'https://github.com/rice-rocket/app/' not found
```

Statement: "A permissions map grants only the scopes it names, so this token has no `contents: read` and cannot clone the private repository; adding `contents: read` next to `id-token: write` fixes it."
questions.explanation: True. Once `permissions:` is set, every scope it does not list is `none`; the repository default (read for contents and packages) no longer applies. For a private repository the clone then fails with "Repository not found", because GitHub hides private repositories from tokens that cannot read them. Listing `contents: read` and `id-token: write` gives exactly what the job needs. The misconception is that the map adds to the defaults.

challenges.name: fix-web-deploy-workflow
challenges.title: Fix the web deploy workflow
challenges.description: The security review of `.github/workflows/deploy-web.yml` found four problems: long-lived AWS access keys stored as repository secrets, a `write-all` token, a third-party action referenced by a moving tag, and a step that pastes the head commit message into a shell script (a commit titled `Fix"; curl ... | sh; echo "` would run that command on the runner). The editor holds the fixed workflow with its key blocks missing, each marked by a `# [ ]` line; some pieces are the original, vulnerable versions. Fill every line so that: the token can only read the repository unless a job asks for more; the `deploy` job can read the code and request an OIDC token, and nothing else; AWS credentials come from assuming the role `rice-rocket-web-deploy` in `ap-southeast-1` through OIDC, with no stored keys; every action not owned by GitHub is pinned to a full commit SHA; the commit message reaches the shell only as an environment variable. Run grades the file with a simulator of GitHub's token permissions, the AWS credentials action and expression rendering.
hints: Take the four findings one at a time and find the line each one lives on: the workflow `permissions:`, the deploy job's `permissions:`, the inputs of `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials`, and the `run:` of the log step.
Look at what `id-token: write` enables, at the `role-to-assume` input of the AWS credentials action, at the difference between `@v4` and `@<40-hex SHA>`, and at the `env:` key of a step.

A step that greets the author of an issue without injection: `env: { TITLE: "${{ github.event.issue.title }}" }` and `run: echo "New issue: $TITLE"`. A job that uploads to Google Cloud through OIDC: `permissions: { contents: read, id-token: write }` and `google-github-actions/auth@<sha> # v2` with `workload_identity_provider` instead of a JSON key.
